newsitem.title: ITALY: Mediators detail Burundi peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Mediators detail Burundi peace talks.

text.p: Burundi's government and the country's main Hutu rebel group have agreed to work to restore peace through direct talks on a seven-point agenda aimed at securing a lasting ceasefire, mediators said on Friday.

The Sant'Egidio Community, a Roman Catholic peace group which is based in Rome, confirmed that negotiations between the two sides on ending Burundi's bitter civil war had been taking place in the Italian capital since last December.

It said the direct talks, denied by the government of military ruler Pierre Buyoya until this week, had led to the signing in Rome on March 10 of an accord mapping out a seven-point route to a comprehensive settlement.

The March deal, a copy of which was made available to Reuters, was signed by senior representatives of what the text called the "Government in place in Burundi" and the rebel National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).

"They are continuing to talk. They have begun discussions on the first points of the agenda and we expect the negotiations to continue here in Rome in the coming weeks," Father Matteo Zuppi, a Sant'Egidio mediator, told a news conference.
"The contacts so far suggest to us that there is a real willingness for dialogue," he said.
More than 150,000 people have died in Burundi since October 1993 when the country's first freely-elected president was murdered by Tutsi troops in an attempted coup.

The accord said the government and the CNDD were conscious that the conflict since 1993 was tearing the country apart and were "convinced that the best way to resolve the differences which pit Burundians against each other is negotiation".

"The two parties are determined to search together for the conditions for a return to a durable peace, in dignity and respect for the rights of all Burundians and in conformity with universally accepted fundamental human rights," it said.
The seven points of the negotiating agenda, which the accord says will be treated in turn, are:
-- Restoration of constitutional and institutional order
-- Issues relating to Burundi's armed forces and police
-- A suspension of hostilities
-- Justice, including the creation of an international criminal tribunal to judge acts of genocide and political crimes
-- Identifying and involving other parties in the process
-- A ceasefire
-- Guarantees of how the overall accord should be carried out and respected.

Buyoya confirmed for the first time on Tuesday that direct talks with the CNDD, led by former interior minister Leonard Nyangoma, were under way. Buyoya, who took power in an army coup last July, said the two sides had "agreed all the steps necessary to get a ceasefire".
Senior officials had previously denied the contacts, fearing a backlash from extremist Tutsis.

Buyoya's announcement has been followed by expressions of strong support for the talks from the international community in an effort to bolster the delicate process against any attempts by hardliners to wreck negotiations.
U.S. special envoy Howard Wolpe said on Thursday that "anyone who would seek to interfere with the process should receive the condemnation of the international community".
He was echoed on Friday by Norway, which the Sant'Egidio said was supporting its mediation efforts financially.

"These talks are the most hopeful in the whole of the Central African region where one conflict has followed another and where political willingness to negotiate has been sorely missing," Norwegian Deputy Foreign Minister Jan Egeland said.
"The international community should commend the parties and warn any extremist groups against derailing the peace effort."

Sant'Egidio, which mediated a peace accord for Mozambique in 1992, said its action on Burundi was intended to support wider efforts by former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere to involve all parties in Burundi in the peace process.

Zuppi said Nyerere was expected to convene a dialogue in the coming weeks among the various parties, including the mainly Tutsi UPRONA party and the predominantly Hutu FRODEBU party as well as the government, the CNDD and other forces.
The March 10 accord was signed for the government by Bernard Barandereka, the energy and mines minister, and for the CNDD by Leonce Ndarubagiye.
